papers.title: Not All Layers Need Tuning: Selective Layer Restoration Recovers Diversity
papers.quote: restoring a carefully chosen range of layers to their pre-trained weights can recover diversity while maintaining high output quality
papers.relation: Weight-level restoration of whole layer ranges chosen by a proxy task, measured on output diversity. We restore specific READOUT ROWS (the fork-class unembedding rows) and single / joint late-MLP weights at one algorithm fork, with matched-norm random-row, delta-transplant and residual-subspace nulls, matched early swaps and same-layer random deltas; our W2 result (late MLPs do not beat matched early swaps) is a cautionary control for layer-range restoration claims.

papers.title: The RLVR Policy Shift Is Sparse and Predictable from the Base Model
papers.quote: We introduce Fork-Patched Decoding (FPD), a decoder that splices base logits into the trained policy where the gate fires.
papers.relation: Token-level baseline. We rerun FPD at the counterfactual fork (base fp32 fork logits) beside our weight-level arm: FPD gives 15/30 correct DFS on CC (iteration 9: 18/30) while restoring the three fork-class rows gives 5/30.

papers.title: Sparse but Critical: A Token-Level Analysis of Distributional Shifts in RLVR Fine-Tuning of LLMs
papers.quote: RL fine-tuning induces highly sparse and targeted changes, with only a small fraction of token distributions exhibiting meaningful divergence
papers.relation: Token-swap cross-sampling between base and RL generations; we work at a single decision token and ask which WEIGHTS hold the instruct default there.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning Enhances Existing Mechanisms: A Case Study on Entity Tracking
papers.authors: Prakash, Rott Shaham, Haklay, Belinkov, Bau
papers.quote: fine-tuning enhances, rather than fundamentally alters, the mechanistic operation of the model
papers.relation: Activation-level cross-model patching (iteration 9's B2 used CMAP and found it non-specific at the MST fork); W1 is the weight-level complement at the readout.

papers.title: Check Your LLM's Secret Dictionary! Five Lines of Code Reveal What Your LLM Learned
papers.quote: Base-instruct comparison reveals that ethically concerning subspaces originate in pretraining and are not removed by post-training alignment.
papers.relation: lm_head structure across base/instruct and families; consistent with our family dependence: the Qwen fork-class rows carry about half (CC) or more than all (MST) of the gap, the Gemma output-untied rows widen it (W3, descriptive).

papers.title: The Unlocking Spell on Base LLMs: Rethinking Alignment via In-Context Learning
papers.quote: base LLMs and their alignment-tuned versions perform nearly identically in decoding on the majority of token positions. Most distribution shifts occur with stylistic tokens.
papers.relation: Token-distribution shift between base and aligned models; our forks are decision (algorithm) tokens, not stylistic ones, and we localise the shift at the weight level.

papers.title: Layer Swapping for Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Transfer in Large Language Models
papers.quote: this layer swapping is simple, inexpensive, and intuitive, as it is based on an interpretative analysis of the most important parameter changes
papers.relation: Module swaps between fine-tuned experts for capability transfer; methodologically related to our W2 module swaps, which add matched-norm and same-layer random-delta controls.

summary: No paper found that restores fork-class unembedding rows of the base model into the instruct readout with matched-norm null rows and a common-random-number generation test; the closest are SLR (layer-range restoration for diversity) and FPD (token-level base-logit splicing), both adjacent.
